name: Sara Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Sara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It depends on the month, but today I was lambing from five. We farm Greystone, which is about 200 hectares, sheep and wheat with some oilseed, and I run it with two full-time staff and a student in spring. My husband Jun teaches at the primary school in town, so mornings are a bit of a race with Mika and Hana's lunchboxes. Afternoons are fieldwork, and twice a week I do the farm shop's accounts.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any technology on the farm day to day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Some. The tractor steers itself on GPS, which I fought for two years before I gave in, and now I'd never go back. I'll ask one of those AI chat tools now and then to check a spray rule or draft a letter to the council. I'm not first in the queue for anything, but once my neighbour's tried it and not lost a field, I'll listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now we can talk about what actually matters, which is fair prices and the supermarkets squeezing us. I'd probably joke about it in the machinery-sharing group chat. Someone would post a meme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a little disappointed. The letter-writing and the spray records are the dull parts, and I'd hoped to hand those off. But the farm itself would be fine, and so would Ray and Colin, my two lads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Keep using the chat tool for paperwork, keep the GPS, keep the shop going. I'd probably put the money I'd been saving for new kit into a better lambing shed instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of shrug. Not a lot changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ray and Colin about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably nothing, they'd not care. Colin's 58 and still writes the stock book in pencil. Colin's been waiting thirty years for some machine to replace him, and he's still the best shepherd in the valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any downside for you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big buyers would still squeeze us, AI or no AI. That's the real fight. I'd still be on at the farmers' union about the supermarket contracts.

S0.say: I'd say good, now we can get back to what matters, which is fair prices and the supermarkets squeezing farmers. I'd joke about it in the machinery-sharing group chat with the neighbours.
S0.think: Privately I'd be slightly disappointed, because I'd hoped to hand off the dull paperwork. But the farm and my two workers would be fine.
S0.do: Keeps using the chat tool for paperwork and the GPS steering on the tractor. Puts the money set aside for new kit into a better lambing shed instead, and keeps pushing the farmers' union on supermarket contracts.
S0.feel: Calm, with a shrug; little changes for her.
S0.quote: Colin's been waiting thirty years for some machine to replace him, and he's still the best shepherd in the valley.
S0.fieldNote: Sara sees the real fight as prices and the supermarkets, not AI, and that framing sticks. She's affectionate about Colin, her older shepherd, and uses him to make the point that people have predicted his replacement for decades. Her small disappointment shows she does want some help with paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to share the cost and the gains. Small farms can't each buy a robot weeder, but a machinery ring can, that's a group of farms sharing kit. I'd say the government should help co-ops buy it, the way they help with drainage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think we'd come out of it fine, maybe better. I'm good at what I do and I'm not afraid of a new machine once it's been proven. The worry is the bigger estates getting there first and pushing land rents up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Over the first year I'd get the machinery ring to trial one robot weeder on the wheat, split eight ways. I'd do a short course on the new farm software at the college over winter. And I'd talk to Ray, who's thirty, about whether he wants to be the one who looks after the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a bit uneasy about the big estates. Interested, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not afraid of a machine once it's proven. Who has to prove it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone with more money than me. The Hartley estate down the road will buy anything shiny. I'll let the Hartleys buy the first robot and I'll buy the third one, second-hand, once the bugs are out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Colin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Colin would retire, I think, and he's earned it. I'd want him to train whoever comes next, so what he knows doesn't vanish.

S1.say: I'd say small farms need to share the cost and the gains through machinery rings, groups of farms that share kit. The government should help co-ops buy robots the way it helps with drainage.
S1.think: Privately I think we'd come out fine, maybe better, because I'm good at the job and comfortable with proven machines. The worry is that big estates get there first and push land rents up.
S1.do: Gets the machinery ring to trial a robot weeder on the wheat, shared between eight farms, in the first year. Takes a winter course on farm software at the college and asks her worker Ray whether he wants to run the robots.
S1.feel: Mostly fine and even interested, with some unease about the big estates.
S1.quote: I'll let the Hartleys buy the first robot and I'll buy the third one, second-hand, once the bugs are out.
S1.fieldNote: Sara's instinct is shared ownership: machinery rings, co-ops, public help. She is openly happy to let the rich neighbours go first and buy the third robot second-hand. She plans for both workers, offering Ray a new role and wanting Colin to pass on what he knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be saying we need the government to step in, and fast. Guaranteed income for people put out of work, and rules so land doesn't all end up with whoever owns the most robots. I'd say it at the farmers' union and I'd write to our representative.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think we'd keep the land, because we own most of it, but the farm as a job might go. If a robot fleet can farm 200 hectares for less than Ray and Colin and I cost, the bank will ask why we're not using one. Two years means I can't let someone else go first, there's no time for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the lambing shed straight away and keep that money as cash. I'd go through the accounts with Jun and cut the extras, the second holiday, the new car. I'd sit down with the union and the ring and push for public money to help family farms through it. I'd tell Ray and Colin honestly, before Christmas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops just thinking about telling Colin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does telling Colin hit you hardest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because he taught me to lamb when I was nineteen, on this farm, when it was my dad's. Telling Colin a robot can do his job would feel like telling him his whole life was a rehearsal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the farm shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop might be the bit that lasts, actually. People like buying from a person. I'd keep it open, maybe lean on it more.

S2.say: I'd say the government needs to step in fast with a guaranteed income for people put out of work and rules to stop land piling up with whoever owns the most robots. I'd say it at the farmers' union and write to our representative.
S2.think: Privately I think we'd keep the land because we own most of it, but the farm as a job might go. With only two years, I can't wait for others to try things first.
S2.do: Halts the lambing shed and keeps the money as cash, and cuts household extras like a second holiday and a new car with Jun. Pushes the farmers' union and machinery ring for public help for family farms, and tells her two workers honestly before Christmas.
S2.feel: Alarmed, with her stomach dropping at the thought of telling Colin.
S2.quote: Telling Colin a robot can do his job would feel like telling him his whole life was a rehearsal.
S2.fieldNote: The speed matters most to Sara because her whole approach is to wait for proof, and two years removes that option. Her pain centres on Colin, who taught her to lamb on her father's farm. She sees the farm shop as the human part that might last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if we start now, and I'd say it at every union meeting. I'd want public money for farm co-ops to buy robots together, so it isn't just the estates who own them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is just about enough for me. The first farms would go robot in year two or three, I'd watch them, and I'd move in year four. It's tight, but it's how I always do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd put the shed money into savings and learn the farm management software properly, not just now and then. I'd push the ring to buy shared robots in year three. I'd also talk to Jun about the girls' schooling, because Mika would be choosing subjects by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I could manage it. It feels like a hard winter you can see coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Mika to study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something where people need people. I don't know what that is any more. I used to tell her she could take over the farm, and now I'd be wondering if there'll be a farm to take over that needs her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move in year four. What if the robots are expensive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then that's where the co-op matters. Eight farms can afford what one can't. If the government won't help, we'll do it ourselves.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if we start now. I'd push for public money so farm co-ops can buy robots together and the big estates don't own them all.
S3.think: Privately I think five years just about works for me: I'd watch the first farms switch in years two and three and move in year four. It's tight but it's how I always do things.
S3.do: Moves the shed money into savings and learns the farm management software properly in the first year. Pushes the machinery ring to buy shared robots by year three, and starts talking with Jun about Mika's school subjects.
S3.feel: Anxious but manageable, like a hard winter she can see coming.
S3.quote: I used to tell her she could take over the farm, and now I'd be wondering if there'll be a farm to take over that needs her.
S3.fieldNote: Five years fits Sara's wait-then-follow habit, and she maps out her timing year by year. Her line about Mika taking over the farm is the emotional centre. When the cost question comes up, she falls back on the co-op rather than going it alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's plan it like grown-ups. Retraining paid for, shorter weeks, and the gains from the robots shared through tax. I'd be making that case at the union and probably standing for the parish council.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years suits me. I'd be 53, the mortgage nearly done, and I'd have watched the robots for years before buying. I'd worry more for the girls than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep farming and building the shop over the first few years. I'd get the ring to trial robots around year five, and buy into them by year seven. I'd also take the online course on farm robotics the college keeps advertising, just so I know what I'm looking at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more for the girls than for myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Standing for the parish council is new. Why then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because ten years is long enough for local decisions to matter. Who owns the land, who gets the work. If the robots are coming to our valley, I want to be in the room when we decide who gets the keys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Colin and Ray, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Colin would be long retired, so he's fine. Ray would have ten years to learn the robots, and I'd pay for the course. He'd be the one looking after them.

S4.say: I'd say we have a decade, so we should plan it properly, with paid retraining, shorter weeks and the robots' gains shared through tax. I'd make the case at the union and probably stand for the parish council.
S4.think: Privately I think ten years suits me, since I'd be 53 with the mortgage nearly paid and years to watch the robots before buying. I'd worry more for my daughters than for myself.
S4.do: Keeps farming and grows the farm shop for the first few years. Takes the college's online farm robotics course, plans to trial robots with the machinery ring around year five, and pays for Ray to train on them.
S4.feel: Uneasy, mostly on behalf of her daughters.
S4.quote: If the robots are coming to our valley, I want to be in the room when we decide who gets the keys.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Sara turns local and political, thinking about standing for the parish council. She is calm about her own future and moves her worry onto her daughters. Her plan for Ray shows she thinks of her staff's future as part of her job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I can't wait for proof, and I always wait for proof. What would help is a guaranteed income for farm workers who lose their jobs and public money for co-ops to buy robots, so it's not just the estates who own the future.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Who owns the land. Nobody asked that. If the robots do the work, the only thing left is who owns the ground, and that's the question that'll decide whether my girls are all right.

headlineQuote: I'm not first in the queue for anything, but once my neighbour's tried it and not lost a field, I'll listen.
portrait: Sara Nakamura is 43 and runs Greystone, a sheep and wheat farm she took over from her father, with two staff and a farm shop. She's careful with new technology, waiting for neighbours to prove it, and uses AI tools now and then for paperwork. Her answers keep returning to shared ownership: machinery rings, co-ops and public support for family farms. She's calm in the slower scenarios, alarmed by AGI in two years because it leaves no time to wait for proof, and with ten years she turns to local politics and her daughters' future.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years, because she always waits for proof before changing and there'd be no time to do that.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed income for farm workers who lose their jobs, and public money for co-ops to buy robots together.
